source_book.author: Martin Kleppmann
source_book.source_format: ZIP archive containing a Mobipocket (.mobi) ebook extracted to HTML/plain text plus image files

metadata.purpose: Compact reasoning layer for repeated coding/system-design conversations; not production evidence.
source_limitations: The uploaded source is a MOBI ebook rather than PDF; stable print page numbers are not exposed by the extractor.
Traceability therefore uses chapter, section heading, and MOBI text-character anchors.
Figures were extracted as image files and inventoried by label; figure content was inspected via extracted image files/contact sheets, but not OCR-transcribed into the JSON.
Some ebook glyphs and navigation artifacts are present in extracted text; substantive chapter text and headings are readable.
No outside research was used, so source-era product examples are not modernized.

authority_order: Current production code and system behavior
Current logs, metrics, tests, and incidents
operating_instructions: Treat DDIA as a conceptual map, not project evidence.
Inspect current code, logs, metrics, tests, incidents, and vendor docs first.

Identify source of truth, derived data, read/write paths, transaction boundaries, retries, ordering, consistency, schema evolution, partitioning, replication, batch/streaming, and idempotency assumptions.
Ask for evidence before diagnosing root cause.
Separate source-supported concepts, cross-chapter synthesis, engineering extension, AI-agent extension, and current-verification flags.
Prefer simple designs before distributed coordination, event logs, streaming, or consensus.
Do not claim exactly-once, linearizability, serializability, or vendor-specific behavior without current evidence.
Return concrete tests, observability checks, and tradeoff tables.

core_thesis.thesis_statement: Data-intensive systems should be designed by making data models, storage, communication, replication, partitioning, transactions, and derived-data flows explicit, then evaluating their reliability, scalability, and maintainability tradeoffs under realistic faults and change.
system_design_implications: Start with the data model, read/write paths, and source-of-truth boundaries.
Prefer simple designs until measured load, correctness, or fault-tolerance needs justify added distributed machinery.
Treat compatibility, retries, ordering, and idempotence as design constraints, not afterthoughts.
operational_implications: Instrument lag, retries, duplicates, partitions, aborts, backfills, and source-versus-derived drift.
Plan recovery and reprocessing paths before failures occur.
reliability_implications: Expect faults, partial failure, clock uncertainty, and retries.
Check end-to-end correctness rather than trusting isolated component guarantees.
limitations_or_cautions: The book is conceptual and source-era-specific for named products; current product behavior must be verified.

failure_modes.name: Lost updates
failure_modes.plain: Concurrent read-modify-write cycles overwrite a previous result.
symptoms: counter goes down
edits disappear
inventory count ignores one purchase

failure_modes.name: Dirty reads
failure_modes.plain: A transaction observes data that another transaction has not committed.
symptoms: temporary state leaks
report includes data that disappears
conditions: concurrent transaction has written but not committed

failure_modes.name: Dirty writes
failure_modes.plain: One transaction overwrites another transaction's uncommitted write.
symptoms: committed value depends on race
rollback cannot restore invariant

failure_modes.name: Read skew
failure_modes.plain: A reader sees parts of the database from different points in time.
symptoms: inconsistent report
sum of accounts does not balance
conditions: reader scans while writer updates related objects
tests: repeat same multi-row query during transfer

failure_modes.name: Write skew
failure_modes.plain: Two transactions each make a decision from a snapshot and update different rows, violating a shared rule.
symptoms: invariant broken without direct row conflict
two on-call shifts removed

failure_modes.name: Phantoms
failure_modes.plain: A transaction's predicate would match a row inserted or changed by another transaction.
symptoms: double booking
uniqueness rule violated by concurrent insert
conditions: decision uses absence or count of matching rows

failure_modes.name: Race condition across services
failure_modes.plain: Timing between independently failing services changes the outcome.
symptoms: intermittent duplicates
impossible state
flaky incident reproduction

failure_modes.name: Replication lag
failure_modes.plain: A replica is behind the leader and serves old data.
symptoms: saved value missing
report stale
read after write fails

failure_modes.name: Stale reads after failover
failure_modes.plain: A promoted or selected replica lacks recent acknowledged writes.
symptoms: recent writes vanish
leader change precedes inconsistency

failure_modes.name: Split brain
failure_modes.plain: Two actors believe they are the leader or authority at the same time.
symptoms: double writes
divergent logs
conflicting leaders

failure_modes.name: Clock skew
failure_modes.plain: Different machines disagree about current time or time moves unexpectedly.
symptoms: events appear out of order
TTL expires early
last-write-wins loses newer intent

failure_modes.name: Network partition
failure_modes.plain: Nodes cannot communicate even though some continue running.
symptoms: timeouts
unavailable shard
divergent updates

failure_modes.name: Retry duplication
failure_modes.plain: A retry repeats a side effect because the first attempt may have succeeded.
symptoms: duplicate charge
duplicate row
job effect performed twice

failure_modes.name: Ordering ambiguity
failure_modes.plain: Events are processed in an order that does not match causal expectations.
symptoms: delete before create
status regresses
consumer sees effect before cause

failure_modes.name: Exactly-once misconception
failure_modes.plain: Engineers assume a processing framework prevents all duplicate external effects.
symptoms: duplicate emails
double writes despite exactly-once setting

failure_modes.name: Hot partition
failure_modes.plain: One partition receives disproportionate load.
symptoms: one shard high CPU
p99 latency localized
throttling by key
tests: load test with real key distribution

failure_modes.name: Rebalancing disruption
failure_modes.plain: Moving partitions harms availability or latency during topology change.
symptoms: latency spike during scaling
wrong-node requests
incomplete data movement

failure_modes.name: Schema incompatibility
failure_modes.plain: Old and new components cannot decode each other's data.
symptoms: deploy breaks consumers
old messages unreadable
missing field crash

failure_modes.name: Derived-data inconsistency
failure_modes.plain: Cache, index, view, or warehouse disagrees with the source of truth.
symptoms: report mismatch
search result missing
cache says old state

failure_modes.name: Backfill double count
failure_modes.plain: A reprocessing job counts records already included by incremental processing.
symptoms: metrics jump
duplicate aggregates
historical correction over-applies

failure_modes.name: Stream join timing issue
failure_modes.plain: A join or window misses or misclassifies late/out-of-order events.
symptoms: missing match
late correction
inconsistent dashboard

failure_modes.name: Missing event
failure_modes.plain: A consumer never observes an event required for downstream correctness.
symptoms: state transition absent
warehouse row missing
stuck workflow

failure_modes.name: Duplicate event
failure_modes.plain: The same logical event is processed more than once.
symptoms: duplicate notification
aggregate too high
duplicated projection row

failure_modes.name: Dual-write inconsistency
failure_modes.plain: A workflow writes two systems but only one write succeeds.
symptoms: DB says sent but email not sent
index update missing
tests: compare DB rows to emitted events

failure_modes.name: Quorum overclaim

symptoms: stale quorum read
conflicting versions
surprising conflict resolution

failure_modes.name: Last-write-wins data loss
failure_modes.plain: Conflict resolution by timestamp discards one concurrent write.
symptoms: user update disappears
conflict not surfaced

failure_modes.name: RPC local-call fallacy

retry storm

failure_modes.name: CDC schema break

decision_rules.name: Relational versus document versus graph model
decision_rules.default: Prefer the simplest model that matches relationship shape and update patterns.
choose_when: data is many-to-many or relationship-heavy
document locality is real
graph traversals dominate
avoid_when: the choice is driven only by product fashion or vendor familiarity

decision_rules.name: OLTP versus OLAP separation
decision_rules.default: Keep operational transactions separate until analytic scans demonstrably interfere.
choose_when: analytical queries scan large data or require columnar layouts
user-facing latency suffers
avoid_when: the same database can meet latency and analytical needs with clear evidence

decision_rules.name: B-tree versus log-structured storage
decision_rules.default: Use the storage engine whose write, read, and range-scan profile matches the workload.
choose_when: write throughput and compaction tradeoffs are acceptable
range scans or mature indexing dominate
avoid_when: only the marketing label is known, not measured workload behavior

decision_rules.name: Secondary index budget
decision_rules.default: Add secondary indexes only for access paths that justify write and maintenance cost.
choose_when: queries need alternate lookup fields often enough
freshness requirements are understood
avoid_when: an index duplicates data without an owner or correctness check

decision_rules.name: Encoding format choice
decision_rules.default: Select encodings for compatibility, safety, and independent evolution, not convenience alone.
choose_when: data crosses languages, storage lifetimes, or service deployments
avoid_when: data is strictly local and ephemeral

decision_rules.name: Schema evolution strategy
decision_rules.default: Require old-reader/new-writer and new-reader/old-writer tests for durable or queued data.
choose_when: rolling deploys, retained messages, or old records exist
avoid_when: all components are upgraded atomically and no old data remains

decision_rules.name: Service API versus message boundary
decision_rules.default: Choose synchronous APIs for immediate request/response needs and messages for decoupled durable handoff.
choose_when: producer and consumer should evolve or fail independently
immediate answer is unnecessary
avoid_when: callers require a result before proceeding

decision_rules.name: Single-leader replication
decision_rules.default: Default to single-leader when one write authority is acceptable and simplicity matters.
choose_when: writes can route to one leader
failover semantics are acceptable
avoid_when: offline or multi-region writes are mandatory

decision_rules.name: Synchronous versus asynchronous replication
decision_rules.default: Use synchronous replication only for data whose acknowledged durability/freshness outweighs latency and availability cost.
choose_when: losing an acknowledged write is unacceptable
replicas are close enough
avoid_when: latency or availability dominates and occasional lag is tolerable

decision_rules.name: Multi-leader replication
decision_rules.default: Use multi-leader only when accepting local writes in multiple places is worth conflict handling.
choose_when: offline clients or multi-datacenter writes require local acceptance
avoid_when: conflicts cannot be merged or surfaced

decision_rules.name: Leaderless replication
decision_rules.default: Use leaderless/quorum systems only after checking actual consistency semantics under failure.
choose_when: availability and write acceptance under failures matter
conflict handling is designed
avoid_when: the team expects simple single-copy behavior

decision_rules.name: Partition key selection
decision_rules.default: Choose partition keys from observed access and load distribution, not just entity identity.
choose_when: data exceeds one node
key distribution is measured
avoid_when: single-node capacity is enough or keys are highly skewed with no mitigation

decision_rules.name: Range versus hash partitioning
decision_rules.default: Prefer range partitioning for range locality and hash partitioning for even distribution.
choose_when: range scans dominate
uniform load dominates
avoid_when: the workload needs both without a secondary strategy

decision_rules.name: Rebalancing strategy
decision_rules.default: Require throttled, observable, reversible rebalancing before relying on elastic scale.
choose_when: cluster size or load changes
partitions must move
avoid_when: static capacity is enough and movement risk outweighs benefit

decision_rules.name: Transaction boundary choice
decision_rules.default: Put operations in one transaction when they maintain the same invariant and share a database boundary.
choose_when: partial success would violate business rules
avoid_when: steps are independent and can be compensated safely

decision_rules.name: Isolation level choice
decision_rules.default: Select isolation by the anomalies the workflow cannot tolerate, not by name alone.
choose_when: lost update, read skew, write skew, or phantom can break correctness
avoid_when: weak anomalies only affect noncritical analytics and are accepted

decision_rules.name: Serializability versus performance
decision_rules.default: Use serializable isolation when correctness depends on cross-row predicates or complex invariants.
choose_when: concurrency anomalies are costly or hard to detect
avoid_when: contention or latency cost is too high and weaker controls suffice

decision_rules.name: Timeout and retry policy
decision_rules.default: Treat timeouts as uncertain outcomes and pair retries with idempotency or reconciliation.
choose_when: remote operation has side effects and may have succeeded
avoid_when: operation is read-only or inherently idempotent and documented

decision_rules.name: Lease and leader safety
decision_rules.default: Use fencing tokens when an old leader could continue acting after pause or partition.
choose_when: shared resource accepts writes from leader-like actors
avoid_when: the resource itself rejects stale epochs

decision_rules.name: Linearizable operation selection
decision_rules.default: Reserve linearizability for operations that truly require single-copy current behavior.
choose_when: uniqueness, locks, leader election, or immediate visibility matters
avoid_when: session-level or eventual behavior is enough

decision_rules.name: Consensus introduction
decision_rules.default: Introduce consensus through a well-understood coordination service when shared decisions must survive faults.
choose_when: leader election, membership, or config must be agreed
avoid_when: the problem can be solved with one database transaction or static config

decision_rules.name: Distributed transaction decision
decision_rules.default: Avoid distributed transactions unless atomic commit across resources is the core requirement.
choose_when: participants must commit or abort together and blocking risk is acceptable
avoid_when: saga, outbox, reconciliation, or single database boundary is enough

decision_rules.name: Batch versus streaming
decision_rules.default: Use batch when bounded, repeatable input can meet freshness needs; use streaming when latency or continuous reaction matters.
choose_when: freshness requirements exceed batch interval
replay is needed
avoid_when: batch output is simpler and timely enough

decision_rules.name: Batch output publication
decision_rules.default: Publish batch results atomically or by complete generation replacement.
choose_when: readers depend on coherent output
avoid_when: partial intermediate output is never visible

decision_rules.name: Event log versus mutable table
decision_rules.default: Use an event log when order, replay, and integration are first-class needs; use mutable tables for direct current-state queries.
choose_when: multiple consumers need durable change history
avoid_when: only current state is needed and change history adds confusion

decision_rules.name: CDC versus polling
decision_rules.default: Prefer CDC when changes must be complete and ordered from the database log.
choose_when: polling can miss changes or overload the database
avoid_when: rough freshness is enough and missed intermediate states are acceptable

decision_rules.name: Stream partitioning and ordering
decision_rules.default: Partition streams by the entity that requires ordered processing.
choose_when: per-entity order matters
throughput needs partitions
avoid_when: global order is required and cannot be approximated

decision_rules.name: Idempotent processing
decision_rules.default: Make every retryable or replayable side effect idempotent or deduplicated by durable identity.
choose_when: timeouts, replays, redelivery, or backfills are expected
avoid_when: the operation is provably read-only

decision_rules.name: Derived data strategy
decision_rules.default: Treat caches, indexes, warehouses, and materialized views as derived unless explicitly authoritative.
choose_when: data can be rebuilt from source
views serve specialized queries
avoid_when: the projection is the only record of business truth

decision_rules.name: Simplicity before distributed coordination
decision_rules.default: Prefer the least distributed design that meets measured correctness and load requirements.
choose_when: current evidence does not require multi-node coordination
avoid_when: a clear requirement demands fault-tolerant shared decisions
